content: Uranium is a dense, silvery-white metallic element that belongs to the actinide series of the periodic table. It has the chemical symbol U and an atomic number of 92, meaning it contains 92 protons and 92 electrons, with six of these being valence electrons. The number of neutrons in uranium can range from 141 to 146, with isotopes containing 143 and 146 neutrons being the most common. Uranium has the highest atomic weight of all naturally occurring elements and is approximately 70% denser than lead. It is weakly radioactive and occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. Commercially, uranium is extracted from uranium-bearing minerals such as uraninite. Uranium undergoes slow radioactive decay by emitting alpha particles. The half-life of uranium-238 is approximately 4.47 billion years, while that of uranium-235 is 704 million years. These long half-lives make uranium isotopes useful for dating the age of the Earth and other geological formations through methods such as uranium-thorium, uranium-lead, and uranium-uranium dating. Uranium is one of three fissile elements, alongside thorium and plutonium, meaning it can undergo nuclear fission to produce lighter elements. While uranium-238 has a low probability of undergoing fission spontaneously or when bombarded with fast neutrons, uranium-235 and, to a lesser extent, uranium-233 have a much higher probability of fission when bombarded with slow neutrons. This property is exploited in nuclear reactors to generate heat for power production and in nuclear weapons to produce explosive energy. Both applications rely on uranium's ability to sustain a nuclear chain reaction. Depleted uranium, which is primarily uranium-238, is used in military applications such as kinetic energy penetrators and armor plating due to its high density and hardness. It is also used as a shielding material for radioactive containers and as counterweights in aircraft and missiles. Despite its weak radioactivity, the primary health risk from depleted uranium exposure is chemical toxicity rather than radiation. Historically, uranium was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the planet Uranus. The first isolation of uranium metal was achieved by Eugène-Melchior Péligot in 1841. Its radioactive properties were identified in 1896 by Antoine Becquerel. Research by Enrico Fermi and others in the 1930s led to the use of uranium as a nuclear fuel and in the development of nuclear weapons, including the Little Boy bomb dropped on Hiroshima in 1945. During the Cold War, vast stockpiles of uranium were amassed for nuclear weapons production, leading to concerns about the security of these materials after the Soviet Union's dissolution. Uranium mining and production have also raised environmental and health concerns, particularly in regions where mining activities have left behind contamination. Uranium is naturally found in low concentrations in all rocks, soils, and water. It is the heaviest naturally occurring element in significant quantities on Earth and is always found combined with other elements. Its decay contributes to the Earth's internal heat, driving mantle convection and plate tectonics. Uranium is more abundant than elements like silver and mercury and is found in minerals such as uraninite, autunite, and coffinite. Uranium mining is conducted through various methods, including open-pit mining, underground mining, and in-situ leaching. The extracted ore is processed to produce a concentrated form known as yellowcake, which contains uranium oxides. This material is further refined and converted for use in nuclear reactors or weapons. High-grade uranium ores, such as those found in Canada's Athabasca Basin, can contain up to 70% uranium oxides. Uranium compounds exhibit a range of oxidation states, with uranium(IV) and uranium(VI) being the most common. Uranium dioxide (UO₂) and uranium trioxide (UO₃) are the primary oxides, with uranium dioxide being widely used as nuclear reactor fuel. Uranium oxides are generally stable and insoluble in water, making them suitable for storage and disposal. In aqueous chemistry, uranium ions exist in various oxidation states, including U³⁺, U⁴⁺, UO₂⁺, and UO₂²⁺. The uranyl ion (UO₂²⁺) is particularly significant and forms complexes with carbonate, chloride, and sulfate ions. These interactions influence uranium's behavior in natural and industrial processes. Uranium's applications extend beyond energy and weaponry. It has been used historically as a colorant in glass and ceramics, as well as in photographic chemicals and dyes. Its radioactive properties have also enabled its use in scientific research and radiometric dating.
